skills.name: Write chemical equations including state symbols

note.text:
State symbols are written after each formula to show the physical state:
• (s) solid  • (l) pure liquid  • (g) gas  • (aq) dissolved in water (aqueous)
Examples:
Zn(s) + H2SO4(aq) → ZnSO4(aq) + H2(g)
NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)
Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) → PbI2(s) + 2KNO3(aq)
They are useful because they tell you what would be seen: an (s) formed from (aq) solutions is a precipitate, a (g) means bubbles, and water formed in a neutralisation is (l), not (aq).
A full equation is balanced first, then the state symbols are added.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to add state symbols to a balanced equation and use them to say what would be seen.
Builds on: Lesson {28} (balancing) and Form Three states of matter.
Leads to: writing the full equations required in examinations, and ionic equations in Form Five.

sections.heading: The four symbols
sections.text:
A state symbol is written just after each formula:
• (s) solid  • (l) pure liquid  • (g) gas  • (aq) aqueous, that is dissolved in water.
Take care with (l) and (aq). Water made in a neutralisation is {formula('H2O')}(l), because it is water itself. Salt dissolved in water is {formula('NaCl')}(aq), because it is dissolved IN water.
Write the equation and balance it first; the state symbols are added last, and never change the balancing.

sections.heading: Reading what would be seen
sections.text:
State symbols turn an equation into a description of the experiment.
• {formula('Zn')}(s) + {formula('H2SO4')}(aq) → {formula('ZnSO4')}(aq) + {formula('H2')}(g): the solid disappears and bubbles are given off.
• {formula('Pb(NO3)2')}(aq) + {2}{formula('KI')}(aq) → {formula('PbI2')}(s) + {2}{formula('KNO3')}(aq): two clear solutions give a yellow precipitate.
• {formula('NaOH')}(aq) + {formula('HCl')}(aq) → {formula('NaCl')}(aq) + {formula('H2O')}(l): nothing is seen at all, though the mixture warms up.
So an (s) among (aq) substances means a precipitate, and a (g) means bubbles.

key_words.meaning: an insoluble solid formed when two solutions are mixed
the reaction of an acid with a base to give a salt and water

mistake.wrong: the water made in a neutralisation is written {formula('H2O')}(aq)
mistake.why: (aq) means dissolved in water; water cannot be dissolved in itself.

worked_example.problem: Write the equation, with state symbols, for adding dilute hydrochloric acid to solid calcium carbonate.
steps: The reactants are solid calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid solution.
A carbonate with an acid gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide.
Then add the states: the carbonate is (s), the acid and the salt are (aq), the water is (l) and the carbon dioxide is (g).

pick.q: What does the state symbol (aq) mean?
pick.r: Dissolved in water: an aqueous solution
e: A pure liquid is shown by (l), such as water itself.

pick.q: Which state symbol is used for water formed in a neutralisation at room temperature?
e: (aq) is for a substance DISSOLVED in water, not for water itself.
Water is a gas only above {100} °C.
Water is a solid only below {0} °C.
pick.y: Water at room temperature is a pure liquid, so it takes (l).

pick.q: Why are state symbols useful in an equation?
pick.r: They show what would be seen: a precipitate, a gas given off, or a clear solution
w: They give the mass of each substance
They show how fast the reaction goes
e: Balancing is done with coefficients; state symbols do not affect it.
Masses come from the moles and the molar masses.
Speed is not shown by an equation at all.

pick.q: Put the steps of writing a full chemical equation in order.
s: Name the reactants and the products
Write the correct formula for each one
Balance the equation by changing the coefficients only
Count every element again to check
Add the state symbols after each formula

pick.q: Put these steps of predicting what will be seen in order.
s: Write the balanced equation with state symbols
Look for an (s) among the products of (aq) reactants
If there is one, expect a precipitate
Look for a (g) among the products
If there is one, expect bubbles of gas

pick.q: Put the steps of working out a mass from an equation in order.
s: Change the mass given into moles
Use the mole ratio from the equation
Change the moles of the product into a mass
Write the answer with its unit
